name: Yara Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive an old hatchback and run three apps at once: one for takeaway food, one for supermarket shopping, one for small parcels. I start around ten, sit in the retail park car park and juggle offers. I'm still not great at it; I accept a bad one maybe twice a day and lose an hour across town. I finish after the late food rush, about eleven.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle of it, honestly, stacking orders so the car is never empty. I use an AI chat app every day to work out which offers pay best per mile and to translate notes from customers. What wears me out is fuel prices and the car, which has 190,000 miles on it. My partner Jonah makes coffee at a café in town, and we've got about three weeks of rent saved, never more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest, because I like the tools. But I'd also post that the real fight is still pay and fuel costs for drivers. If AI isn't going to change much, the apps owe us better rates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the stuff I already use stays useful and nothing much else moves. I'm still stuck at the bottom of the pay scale with a dying car. Most of what I earn goes on keeping the car alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running three apps and use AI to squeeze every mile. I'd go to the meetings for the drivers' co-op idea that's floating around, an app owned by the drivers themselves. I'd try to put twenty a week aside for the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless. Juggling three delivery apps is like being good at a game that doesn't pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said three weeks of rent saved. What happens if the car dies in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't work. No car, no income, and there's nothing else like this round here. I'd borrow from my sister and probably try a bike for food only, which pays maybe half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to be in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not still in that car park. Maybe helping run the co-op app, the tech side. I'd like a job where being good with these tools actually pays.

say: I'm a little **disappointed**, because I like the AI tools.
The real fight is still **pay and fuel** for drivers, so apps owe better rates.
think: I stay at the bottom of the **pay scale** with a dying car.
Most of my earnings go on **keeping the car** alive.
do: Keep running **three apps** and use AI to maximise pay per mile.
Attend meetings about a **drivers' co-op** app.
Put **twenty a week** aside for car repairs.
feel: **Restless**, skilled at a game that doesn't pay.
S0.quote: Juggling three delivery apps is like being good at a game that doesn't pay.
fieldNote: Her stress is the **old car** and thin savings, not technology.
She is **unusually keen** on AI tools for a junior driver, using them daily.
Sees a **drivers' co-op** as both politics and a career path.

steps.text: Keep running the food, shopping and parcel apps together
Use an AI chat app to rank offers by pay per mile
Go to the drivers' co-op app meetings
Set aside twenty a week for car repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn the tools before they learn you. I'd post tips for other drivers on how to use AI to read offers and plan routes, because the apps already do it against us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my driving is fine for a few years, but the juggling part I'm good at gets done by the apps themselves. If the delivery app stacks orders for me perfectly, my one edge is gone. And there'd be more drivers, because office people would need work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a short online course in fleet dispatch, the people who manage delivery vans and robots. I'd keep driving. I'd help set up the drivers' co-op, maybe as the person who sorts the tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and nervous in the same breath. Mostly nervous about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Most of your day is driving, but you also juggle offers. Does the thinking AI side touch you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the planning is the thinking part, and the apps will do it better than my chat app. Then all that's left of my job is the steering wheel and the stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Jonah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah's café is safe-ish, coffee is hands-on. Jonah's hours already got cut when the café put in a self-order screen, though, so I'm not counting on it.

say: Drivers should **learn the tools** before the tools learn them.
I'd post **AI tips** for drivers, since apps already use it against them.
think: My edge in **juggling offers** gets absorbed by the apps themselves.
Office workers needing jobs would mean **more drivers** competing.
do: Take a short online course in **fleet dispatch**.
Help build the **drivers' co-op**, handling the tech side.
feel: **Excited and nervous** together, mainly nervous about money.
S1.quote: If the delivery app stacks orders for me perfectly, my one edge is gone.
fieldNote: She spots that the **thinking part** of her job is exactly what she's best at.
Adaptive instinct: she moves **towards dispatch** rather than away from tech.
Partner's café hours were already cut by a **self-order screen**.

steps.text: Complete an online fleet dispatch course
Keep driving the three apps for income
Set up the tech side of the drivers' co-op

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a basic income and fast, and the companies that own the robots should pay for it. I'd go to protests. Nobody was ready for this, including the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dispatch and planning go first, in 2028, so my course would be useless before I finished it. Then robot cars and pavement robots take the driving around 2031. I'd be 30 with nothing, unless I land something in the robot side itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get hired by whoever runs the robot fleets, as a remote helper who unsticks robots that get confused. I'd drive as much as I can until then and save everything. I'd join every protest for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Proper scared, and a bit angry. I tried to keep up with every new tool, and AGI in two years still might make none of that matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots for hands-on work come about three years after the thinking AI. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years is when I'd make my move, while humans are still needed to babysit the robots. I've read that remote operators watch ten robots at a time. That job might exist only for a few years, but a few years is something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out and my phone plan, then I'd sell the car the day I get a fleet job. Jonah and I would move somewhere cheaper, maybe to his parents' town.

say: A **basic income** is needed fast, paid for by robot owners.
I'd join **protests**, because nobody, including the government, was ready.
think: Driving goes around **2031**, leaving me with nothing unless I join the robot side.
do: Apply to robot fleet firms as a **remote operator**.
Drive and **save everything** until the move.
feel: **Scared** and angry that keeping up might not matter.
S2.quote: I tried to keep up with every new tool, and AGI in two years still might make none of that matter.
fieldNote: She uses the **three-year gap** to aim for remote robot operator work.
Knows such roles may be **short-lived**, and goes for them anyway.
Ready to **move** to Jonah's parents' town to cut costs.

steps.text: Apply to robot fleet firms as a remote operator
Save every spare pound from extra driving shifts
Move with Jonah to his parents' cheaper town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to retrain, if training is free and paid. I'd push the union and the co-op to demand that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years changes it for me. Thinking AI in 2031, robots around 2034. I could learn robot repair, the hands-on fixing, which might be one of the last jobs to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do an evening course in electrics and electronics at the college. I'd use AI tutors to fast-track it. I'd keep driving until I'm qualified and then go after the robot depots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but it's the good kind of nervous. Like before a driving test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the dispatch course would be useless with two years. Is five different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Driving at night and weekends, and maybe the college's grant if I qualify. My chat app has already helped me find two grants I didn't know existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister thinks I'm mad, retraining for the robots that took my job. My view is that the robots that take my delivery job will still need someone with a screwdriver.

say: **Five years** is enough to retrain, if training is free.
I'd push the union and co-op to **demand** paid training.
think: Thinking AI in **2031** and robots around 2034 give me room.
**Robot repair** might be one of the last jobs to go.
do: Take an evening course in **electrics and electronics**.
Use **AI tutors** to move through the course faster.
feel: **Nervous** in a good way, like before a driving test.
S3.quote: The robots that take my delivery job will still need someone with a screwdriver.
fieldNote: Five years turns her into a **planner** aiming at robot repair.
She uses AI to find **grants** and tutors, practical and self-directed.
Her thin savings keep her **anxious** despite a clear plan.

steps.text: Enrol in evening electrics and electronics at the college
Use AI tutors and grant searches to speed up study
Drive nights and weekends until qualified

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where workers can win, if we organise. Ten years is time to build co-ops and get a fair share of what the robots earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a real chance. I'd be 37 when the robots arrive in 2039. I could be a qualified technician by then, maybe running a small repair team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend a year getting the car sorted and saving, then start the electronics course. I'd use AI every day to study. I'd keep working on the drivers' co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. Uneasy that money still runs out every month right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still go for robot repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and more. With ten years I could learn the software side too, not just the screwdriver. I'd want to be the one the robot companies can't do without.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Today. The car, the rent, the fuel. A decade is great, but my rent is due in eleven days.

say: **Ten years** is time for workers to win if they organise.
Co-ops could give drivers a **fair share** of what robots earn.
think: I'd be **37** when the robots arrive in 2039.
I could be a **qualified technician**, maybe leading a small repair team.
do: Spend a year fixing the **car** and saving.
Start the **electronics course** with daily AI study help.
feel: Mostly **hopeful**, but uneasy about money running out monthly.
S4.quote: A decade is great, but my rent is due in eleven days.
fieldNote: The long timeline makes her **hopeful**; her plan is ambitious and specific.
Today's **rent and car** remain the drag on her mood.
Wants to learn the **software side** too, not just repair.

steps.text: Fix the hatchback and build a small cushion first
Train as a robot technician, hardware and software
Keep building the drivers' co-op app

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be halfway through retraining for something that disappears. What would help is free courses with a living allowance, and the robot firms having to hire and train people from the jobs they replace.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask if I want to keep driving. I don't, really. I want to be the person who makes the delivery system work, not the person running up stairs with someone's pizza at eleven at night.

headlineQuote: I want to be the person who makes the delivery system work, not the person running up stairs with someone's pizza at eleven at night.
portrait: Yara is **27**, runs three delivery apps from an ageing hatchback and lives with a café worker.
She uses **AI tools daily** to pick offers, and enjoys the puzzle of stacking orders.
She expects apps to absorb her **planning edge**, so she aims for dispatch, remote operation or robot repair.
Her **progressive** side shows in her support for a drivers' co-op and a basic income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her retraining would be outrun before she finished.
whatWouldHelp: **Free courses** with a living allowance, and robot firms hiring from jobs they replace.
